title: Starting a hot compost heap from cold materials
subtitle: Building and activating a new heap so it reaches 55°C within 48 hours
excerpt: A hot compost heap needs the right ratio of browns to greens, enough moisture, and enough volume to generate heat. Built correctly from cold materials, it should reach 55°C within 48 hours and hold that temperature for the turn cycle. This describes the build and the activation checks.
sourceNotes: US Composting Council guidelines on thermophilic composting; WRAP (Waste and Resources Action Programme) guidance on home composting temperatures; RHS guidance on hot composting.

glossaryTerms.definition: A composting method where the heap is managed to reach and maintain temperatures of 55–70°C, which kills weed seeds and pathogens and breaks down material in 4–8 weeks rather than months.
The ratio of carbon-rich (brown) materials to nitrogen-rich (green) materials in a compost heap. A ratio of roughly 25–30:1 carbon to nitrogen is optimal for fast decomposition.

content.text: A
hot compost
heap needs three things to heat: the right
C:N ratio
, adequate moisture, and enough mass to hold heat. Get all three right at the start and the heap heats itself within 48 hours. Get one wrong and the heap sits cold and slow no matter what you add.
The material requirements before you build
Minimum 1 m³ of total material. Smaller heaps lose heat as fast as they generate it. A cubic metre is roughly 200 litres of kitchen waste plus a similar volume of browns.

A roughly 3:1 mix by volume of brown materials (cardboard, straw, wood chip, dry leaves) to green materials (kitchen waste, fresh grass, green plant trimmings). By weight the mix is closer to 2:1 greens to browns because greens are denser.
Moisture: the heap should feel like a wrung-out sponge. Dry material produces no microbial heat. Waterlogged material goes anaerobic and smells rather than composting.
The build sequence
Start with a 100–150 mm layer of coarse brown material on the ground: wood chip, woody prunings, or cardboard. This keeps the base aerated.
Add a 100 mm layer of greens — kitchen waste, grass clippings, fresh weeds. Do not fill the bin with greens in one layer; they compact and go anaerobic.
Add a 50–75 mm layer of browns. Water the layer if the material is very dry.
Repeat until the bin is full or the materials are exhausted. Each green layer should be sandwiched between brown layers.
Cover the heap with a lid, tarpaulin, or a layer of cardboard. This retains moisture and heat.
The 48-hour check

Insert a compost thermometer 300 mm into the centre of the heap 24 and 48 hours after building. The centre should be 45–55°C within 24 hours and above 55°C within 48 hours if the C:N ratio and moisture are right. If the temperature stays below 40°C after 48 hours, the heap needs adjustment.
Adjustments if the heap does not heat
Heap feels dry: water thoroughly through the top and turn to distribute moisture.
Heap is mostly browns: add a concentrated nitrogen source — fresh nettles, diluted urine (1:10 with water), or grass clippings. Mix in well.
Heap is mostly greens: the heap may be heating but ventilating its heat through the compacted mass. Break it up with a fork and repack with more brown layers.
Heap is below minimum volume: consolidate into one bay if you have a multi-bin system, or add more material before rechecking.

rows.symptom: Heap heats for two days then cools back to ambient
rows.cause: Oxygen depleted in the centre; microbial activity slows as CO₂ builds up
rows.fix: Turn the heap — move the outer cool material to the centre and the hot centre material to the outside. This reinjects air and restarts the heating cycle.

rows.symptom: Heap smells of ammonia after three days
rows.cause: Too much nitrogen relative to carbon; greens are breaking down and releasing nitrogen as ammonia gas
rows.fix: Add a substantial quantity of browns and turn. Cardboard torn into 100 mm pieces absorbs the excess nitrogen effectively.
